{{Primary sources|date=June 2026}}

'''Ralph D. Lorenz''' is a planetary scientist and engineer at the [[Applied Physics Laboratory|Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Lab]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://secwww.jhuapl.edu/SpaceScience/Staff/ProfileView/51|title=JHUAPL - Ralph, Lorenz - Science Research Portal|website=secwww.jhuapl.edu|access-date=2019-10-27}}</ref> whose research focuses on understanding surfaces, atmospheres, and their interactions on planetary bodies, especially [[Titan (moon)|Titan]], [[Venus]], [[Mars]], and [[Earth]].<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Zacny|first1=K.|last2=Lorenz|first2=R.|last3=Rehnmark|first3=F.|last4=Costa|first4=T.|last5=Sparta|first5=J.|last6=Sanigepalli|first6=V.|last7=Mank|first7=Z.|last8=Yen|first8=B.|last9=Yu|first9=D.|last10=Bailey|first10=J.|last11=Bergman|first11=D.|title=2019 IEEE Aerospace Conference |chapter=Application of Pneumatics in Delivering Samples to Instruments on Planetary Missions |date=2019|chapter-url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8741887/authors#authors|pages=1–13|doi=10.1109/AERO.2019.8741887|isbn=978-1-5386-6854-2|s2cid=195222645}}</ref> He currently serves as Mission Architect of  ''[[Dragonfly (Titan space probe)|Dragonfly]]'', NASA's fourth selected [[New Frontiers program|New Frontiers]] mission,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Voosen|first=Paul|date=2019-07-05|title=NASA to fly drone on Titan|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.365.6448.15-a|journal=Science|language=en|volume=365|issue=6448|pages=15.1–15|doi=10.1126/science.365.6448.15-a|issn=0036-8075|pmid=31273103|bibcode=2019Sci...365...15V|s2cid=195807081|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dragonfly.jhuapl.edu/Our-Team/|title=Dragonfly Team|last=JHU APL|date=|website=Dragonfly|language=en|access-date=2019-10-23}}</ref> and as participating scientist on ''[[Akatsuki (spacecraft)|Akatsuki]]'' <ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/topics/solarsystem/features/venus20101119.html|title=NASA - Scientists Chosen to Help on Venus Climate Orbiter|website=www.nasa.gov|language=en|access-date=2019-10-23|archive-date=May 17, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170517163742/https://www.nasa.gov/topics/solarsystem/features/venus20101119.html}}</ref> and ''[[InSight]]''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://nspires.nasaprs.com/external/viewrepositorydocument/cmdocumentid=679202/solicitationId=%7B5E7C7C5C-4CA5-F1E6-A32B-BE7ABE54A32C%7D/viewSolicitationDocument=1/InSight%20Abstracts.pdf|title=InSight Participating Scientist Program (INSTPSP) Abstracts of selected proposals|last=|first=|date=|website=NSPIRES}}</ref> 
He is a Co-Investigator on the SuperCam instrument on the Perseverance rover, responsible for interpreting data from its microphone. He leads the Venus Atmospheric Structure Investigation on the DAVINCI Discovery mission to Venus. He is the recipient of the 2020 International Planetary Probe Workshop (IPPW)  Al Seiff memorial award, and the 2022 American Geophysical Union's Fred Whipple Award for contributions to planetary science.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.agu.org/Fall-Meeting/Pages/Schedule-Events/Named-Lectures#Lorenz|title=Lectures|website=agu.org|access-date=December 28, 2022|archive-date=December 28, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221228044711/https://www.agu.org/Fall-Meeting/Pages/Schedule-Events/Named-Lectures#Lorenz}}</ref>

== Education ==
Lorenz earned a B.Eng. in Aerospace Systems Engineering from the University of Southampton (UK) Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics in 1990. For his thesis "Exploring the Surface of Titan", Lorenz was awarded a PhD in Space Sciences from the University of Kent at Canterbury in 1994. Lorenz spent 1994-2006 at the University of Arizona as a postdoctoral fellow and research scientist. In 2006, he joined the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Lab.<ref name=":2">{{cite web|url=https://www.lpl.arizona.edu/~rlorenz/shortCV|title=Ralph D Lorenz - Curriculum Vitae|website=arizona.edu|access-date=30 August 2023}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://hub.jhu.edu/magazine/2020/spring/dragonfly-mission-to-titan/|title=Destination Titan|last=Spring 2020|first=Dale Keiger / Published|date=2020-03-19|website=The Hub|language=en|access-date=2020-03-25}}</ref>

== Research ==
Lorenz has published over 200 papers on spacecraft exploration of several bodies of the [[Solar System]], using scientific instruments and housekeeping data from engineering systems (such as observing the  Mars environment and a transit of Deimos 
<ref>{{Cite journal|title=A Transit Lightcurve of Deimos, Observed with the InSight Solar Arrays|year=2020|last1=Lorenz|first1=Ralph D.|last2=Lemmon|first2=Mark T.|last3=Mueller|first3=Nils|journal=Research Notes of the American Astronomical Society|volume=4|issue=4|page=57|doi=10.3847/2515-5172/ab8d21|bibcode=2020RNAAS...4...57L|s2cid=219008928|doi-access= free}}</ref>  via the solar array currents on the InSight lander <ref>{{Cite journal|title=Scientific Observations with the InSight Solar Arrays: Dust, Clouds and Eclipses on Mars|year=2020|doi=10.1029/2019EA000992|last1=Lorenz|first1=Ralph D.|last2=Lemmon|first2=Mark T.|last3=Maki|first3=Justin|last4=Banfield|first4=Donald|last5=Spiga|first5=Aymeric|last6=Charalambous|first6=Constantinos|last7=Barrett|first7=Elizabeth|last8=Herman|first8=Jennifer A.|last9=White|first9=Brett T.|last10=Pasco|first10=Samuel|last11=Banerdt|first11=W. Bruce|journal=Earth and Space Science|volume=7|issue=5|article-number=e2019EA000992|pmid=32715027|pmc=7375148|bibcode=2020E&SS....700992L|doi-access=free}}</ref> or measuring the dust and gas in the plumes of Enceladus using Cassini's attitude control system <ref>{{Cite journal|title=Enceladus Plume Density from Cassini Spacecraft Attitude Control Data|year = 2018|pmc = 6278931|last1 = Lorenz|first1 = R. D.|last2 = Burk|first2 = T. A.|journal = Icarus|volume = 300|pages = 200–202|doi = 10.1016/j.icarus.2017.09.003|pmid = 30524143|bibcode = 2018Icar..300..200L}}</ref>). He has conducted field research on dust devils,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.planetary.org/articles/1102-roundup-of-dust-devil-research|title=A Roundup of Dust Devil Research|website=The Planetary Society|access-date=30 August 2023}}</ref> sand dunes and volcanos, exploiting techniques such as kite-borne,<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Compact and inexpensive kite apparatus for geomorphological field aerial photography, with some remarks on operations|year=2014|doi=10.1016/j.grj.2014.06.001|last1=Lorenz|first1=Ralph D.|last2=Scheidt|first2=Stephen P.|journal=Georesj|volume=3-4|pages=1–8|bibcode=2014GeoRJ...3....1L |doi-access=free}}</ref> timelapse and near-infrared photography.  He has also published on the dynamics of Frisbees,<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Flight and attitude dynamics measurements of an instrumented Frisbee|year=2005|doi=10.1088/0957-0233/16/3/017|s2cid=16105503|last1=Lorenz|first1=Ralph D.|journal=Measurement Science and Technology|volume=16|issue=3|pages=738–748|bibcode=2005MeScT..16..738L}}</ref> the thermodynamics of the [[drinking bird]] toy,<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Finite-time thermodynamics of an instrumented drinking bird toy|year=2006|doi=10.1119/1.2190688|last1=Lorenz|first1=Ralph|journal=American Journal of Physics|volume=74|issue=8|pages=677–682|bibcode=2006AmJPh..74..677L}}</ref> and the moving rocks ("Sailing Stones") of [[Racetrack Playa]] in Death Valley.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.earth-surf-dynam-discuss.net/esurf-2014-32/|title=Trail formation by ice-shoved "sailing stones" observed at Racetrack Playa, Death Valley National Park|doi=10.5194/esurfd-2-1005-2014|last1=Lorenz|first1=R. D.|last2=Norris|first2=J. M.|last3=Jackson|first3=B. K.|last4=Norris|first4=R. D.|last5=Chadbourne|first5=J. W.|last6=Ray|first6=J.|journal=Earth Surface Dynamics Discussions|date=28 August 2014|volume=2|issue=2|pages=1005–1022|bibcode=2014ESuDD...2.1005L |doi-access=free }}</ref> He documented the migration of sand dunes at the Mos Espa film set in Tunisia, seen on the Star Wars movies.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.planetary.org/articles/dunes-on-tatooine|title=Dunes on Tatooine|website=The Planetary Society|access-date=30 August 2023}}</ref> 
His contributions in scientific history include noting the calculations of [[Edmond Halley]] on the size of wings needed for human flight,<ref>{{Cite journal|url= https://www.aerosociety.com/publications/jah-edmond-halley-s-aeronautical-calculations-on-the-feasibility-of-manned-flight-in-1691/ |journal=Journal of Aeronautical History|title=Edmond Halley's Aeronautical Calculations on the Feasibility of Manned Flight in 1691|volume=2012|number=2|year=2012}}</ref> and the definition<ref>{{Cite journal|journal=Research Notes of the American Astronomical Society |title=Maunder's Work on Planetary Habitability in 1913: Early Use of the term "Habitable Zone" and a "Drake Equation" Calculation|volume=4|number=79|year=2020|doi=10.3847/2515-5172/ab9831 |last1=Lorenz |first1=Ralph D. |page=79 |bibcode=2020RNAAS...4...79L |s2cid=219930646 |doi-access= free}}</ref>  of the [[circumstellar habitable zone]] by [[Edward Maunder]].

Lorenz has participated in several [[NASA]] and [[European Space Agency|ESA]] missions. He was a Young Graduate Trainee for ESA's ''[[Huygens (spacecraft)|Huygens]]'' from 1990-1991 and continued on as a member of the ''Huygens'' Science Team, designing and building its penetrometer instrument.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> As a member of the ''[[Cassini–Huygens|Cassini]]'' RADAR team,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/missions/cassini/mission/team|title=The Team {{!}} Cassini Mission|last=|first=|date=August 22, 2018|website=NASA Solar System Exploration|access-date=2019-10-23}}</ref> Lorenz led the planning of Titan [[radar]] observations during ''Cassini''<nowiki/>'s 13 year mission in the Saturn system. Lorenz was selected as a participating scientist on the Japanese mission ''[[Akatsuki (spacecraft)|Akatsuki]]'' in 2010<ref name=":0" /> and NASA's ''[[InSight]]'' mission at Mars in 2017.<ref name=":1" />

He has also been involved in numerous mission concepts, including the [[Titan Mare Explorer]] (TiME),<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Stofan |first1=E. |last2=Lorenz |first2=R. |last3=Lunine |first3=Jonathan I. |last4=Bierhaus |first4=E. == Filmography == 
Lorenz has appeared in numerous science documentaries and series, including [[Nova (American TV program)|NOVA]], NASA's Unexplained Files, [[Horizon (British TV programme)|Horizon]], and [[Wonders of the Solar System|Wonders of the Solar System.]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm1985744/|title=Ralph Lorenz|website=[[IMDb]]}}</ref>
